item.title: Why Israel's claims cannot be accepted at face value
item.description:
Why Israel's claims cannot be accepted at face value

Submitted by Faisal Hanif on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 14:00
Any statement from Netanyahu, who has a long and troubling history of twisting the media to serve his agenda, deserves rigorous scrutiny
People walk through the entrance to the BBC’s offices in London on 11 November 2025 (AFP)
Off

Every journalism student learns the same lesson: if your mother says she loves you, check it out. A claim is not a fact until it has been tested, and the more power and self-interest behind it, the more rigorously it should be tested.

A BBC Verify investigation has put that principle to a stark test. It identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military said it was investigating allegations that its forces had killed or injured people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel, but for which no public outcome could be found.

Of the 300 cases examined, only 28 had outcomes published on the Israeli army's website. The BBC says it repeatedly approached the military about the cases but received information on only two, both still under review.

The findings do not establish that every allegation is true or that every investigation should lead to prosecution. They raise a basic question: what value does "Israel says" have if the public is never told the eventual outcome?

Yet in Britain, applying that rule to Israel risks arousing the ire of those whose entire purpose is predicated on promoting or defending the Zionist state narrative.

MP Ayoub Khan, who has been derided as a “Gaza independent” by the British media for his advocacy against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, was recently denounced by a slew of media and politicians for questioning the speed of Israel’s inquiry into the Flydubai incident that resulted in an emergency landing late last month. 

Yet Khan’s refusal to simply accept Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s word deserves to be taken seriously, mainly because the ire was not reserved for him alone. 

The BBC was attacked for adhering to proper editorial standards by putting the word “hero”, used by Netanyahu, in quotation marks in its coverage of the Indian pilot who was stabbed on the Israel-bound flight.

Sam Kiley, an experienced foreign editor for the Independent, was condemned for asking who stood to gain from the incident, daring to suggest that it served Netanyahu as he seeks re-election. 

Netanyahu had warned of potential attacks ahead of the 27 October vote. After the Flydubai incident, both he and Defence Minister Israel Katz said it proved them right. 

Asking who benefits from an event, and from how it is framed, is one of the oldest questions in political analysis. The charge against these critics is that doubt itself reveals prejudice. In reality, it is the other way around: credulity is the failure.

Pushing a narrative

This is not paranoia. It is the historical record.

In 1954, Israeli military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews to bomb British- and American-owned sites in Egypt, intending to blame the attacks on the Muslim Brotherhood and communists. Israel long denied involvement and only honoured the surviving agents in 2005.

Netanyahu's 'eighth front': Israel's billion-dollar war on the truth is failing
Read More »

After the October 2023 Hamas attack, a spokesperson for Netanyahu said babies had been found decapitated. The claim reached British front pages, and former US President Joe Biden said he saw photos of the beheadings. The White House later had to walk back his claim, which has since been debunked. 

The pattern is always the same: a confident assertion that rapidly spreads, becoming part of the folklore that seeks to paint Israel as a perpetual victim, before later being shown to be false.

“Netanyahu says” is a record of what a politician wants the public to believe. “An Israeli official told us” is the same claim with all accountability stripped out. Neither proves anything. That something was said can be reported, but whether it is true must be shown. Relaying it without that additional work is transcription, not journalism.

Remarkably, British news outlets have repeatedly given Israel’s prime minister a megaphone to deride Britain, however absurd his claims. After the UK recognised the state of Palestine, Netanyahu moved to rile an already Islamophobic nation with a jibe about the “Islamic Republic of Britain” - a premise that collapses on the facts: Britain is a constitutional monarchy in which Muslims make up around 6 percent of the population. 

After Britain imposed a settlement trade ban, Netanyahu told the Daily Mail that it had become a “rogue state” under Prime Minister Andy Burnham and accused the Labour government of “appeasing an Islamist-leftist alliance”. He has also reiterated the assertion that Israel helped Britain to thwart an Iranian-backed attack on RAF Fairford, another incident with serious question marks attached.

Where the reporting starts

All of this raises another question: why does an individual facing an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity command so much space in British media? Why is the quote the headline and the evidence an afterthought?

Perhaps Israel’s targeting of major British journalists - including Piers Morgan, Mehdi Hasan and Owen Jones, alongside American commentator Hasan Piker - offers one explanation. All have been, in various ways, critics of Israel’s killing of Palestinian civilians and journalists. Given its well-documented killings of journalists, Israel does not appear to tolerate dissent. 

According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, Israel has killed more than 200 journalists and media workers since October 2023. The committee notes that Israel has repeatedly accused journalists of militant involvement “without producing credible evidence”.

It is reasonable for anyone to ask whether Israel is the ally its supporters describe. Journalists cannot help the public to answer that question if they simply relay its statements verbatim

The cost of deference is self-censorship, and the evidence of it is stark. The Centre for Media Monitoring found the BBC gave a rationale for Israeli military actions in 75 percent of articles on attacks or suffering in Gaza, compared with 17 percent for Russian actions in Ukraine. It challenged Israel’s justifications in 41 percent of cases, compared with 55 percent for Russia. 

The centre also found that the BBC reported the deaths of just 6 percent of 176 Palestinian journalists killed by the Israeli army, compared with 62 percent of journalists in Ukraine. 

With independent journalists barred from Gaza, the world relies on Palestinian reporters and statements from Israeli officials to understand what is happening. If qualifying an Israeli claim brings complaints and political attacks, the response is often silence.

It is reasonable for anyone to ask whether Israel is the ally its supporters describe. Journalists cannot help the public answer that question if they simply relay its statements verbatim. Their job is to scrutinise and challenge. “Israel says” is where the reporting starts, not where it ends.

While brave voices in the trade continue to speak out after three years of genocide in Gaza, “Israel says” remains the routinely used phrase. This is exactly when questions should sharpen.

When trusted media outlets decline to ask the obvious questions, rumours fill the gap. Every question a mainstream newsroom fails to investigate is a question handed to someone who will answer it badly.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

item.title: Morning update
item.description:
Morning update


Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,

If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:

* Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy has said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil struck a sea mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through a “prohibited” area.

* US President Donald Trump says the US Navy is carrying out an effective blockade of Iran and that no Iranian ship has been able to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

* Yemen’s government-aligned forces say 378 Houthi fighters have been killed or wounded in ground clashes and air attacks in Taiz governorate, while the Saudi-led coalition forces claimed two Houthi ballistic missile launchers were destroyed in Yemen’s northern Saada governorate.

*The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said that a tanker has been struck by an unknown projectile 68 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia, on Friday.

* Israeli settlers opened fire at and attacked Palestinian farmers in the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera reported.

*The United Kingdom's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has advised British citizens against all but essential travel to all of  Saudi Arabia.

* Pakistan finance minister says attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.

* Houthi shelling and sniper fire killed a woman and injured five civilians, including a woman and a young girl, in the Sabir al-Mawadim district southeast of Taiz, Al Jazeera reported, citing Yemeni media report.

* Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has called the destruction of ecosystems caused by the "wars of aggression" an act of "ecocide", urging the international community to establish effective and enforceable mechanisms to protect biodiversity during armed conflicts.

* Three US lawmakers have called on the Trump administration to hold Israeli settlers accountable after an attack on Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine and Palestinian villagers in the occupied West Bank. 

* More than half of the minors held in Israeli prisons in 2025 were placed in solitary confinement at least once, including five boys aged 13 to 14, with the vast majority of the children being Palestinians

* The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz because most vessels attacked were refusing to report incidents to the agency.

* Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has said the war on Iran has already cost Europeans more than 100 billion euros ($112bn).

* The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) reports that the number of settler attacks in the West Bank affecting the olive harvest season has already exceeded last year’s number.

* Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police ​and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla ‌activists, Italian prosecutors said on Friday.

item.title: ‘Austerity is inevitably painful’: How Michael Gove justifies his politics | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast
item.description:
For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam

Watch the full episode with Michael Gove here.

Aditya’s suggested reading:

To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair

For slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books

To learn more on what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian

Just why the most successful political party is now failing is analysed in-depth by Phil Burton-Cartledge in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak

Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshall a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch

Geoffrey Wheatcroft does an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!:

or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party

For more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper is acute on how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.

And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, there’s this paper based on data from the Bank of England

Finally, on the Spectator read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in The Guardian

Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?

item.title: Attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure 'worrying' for Pakistan's outlook, minister says
item.description:
Attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure 'worrying' for Pakistan's outlook, minister says

Pakistan's finance minister said on Saturday the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.

In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb told AFP said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.

"We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."

He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.

Since the United States and ally Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.

With Yemen's civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.

Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.

"What is now (the) worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said.

"I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."

Report by AFP

item.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
item.description:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.
